intro: A bassoon begins at the bottom of its range; the violins eventually answer with one of Tchaikovsky’s great love songs. Between them lies a movement capable of turning six pianissimos into an orchestral explosion.

sections.label: Intro · Bassoon and low strings
sections.mNote: A four-note bassoon phrase rises above the double basses

sections.label: A · Violas set the pace
sections.mNote: The bassoon’s phrase becomes a quick, detached viola tune

sections.label: B · The D-major string melody
sections.mNote: Muted violins and cellos sing in long phrases

sections.label: Dev · The orchestra breaks in
sections.mNote: The opening tune is pulled apart in racing string passages

sections.label: B′ · The melody in B major
sections.mNote: The broad string tune returns in the tonic major

sections.label: Coda · Winds over plucked strings
sections.mNote: Descending pizzicato strings accompany the quiet B-major close

cues.title: Bassoon in the depths
cues.text: A bassoon starts low, above double basses that move down by semitones. Its little four-note phrase climbs, tries again higher, then passes to the violas. The symphony begins with instruments usually kept beneath the tune.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, learning resource on Symphony No. 6, pp. 5–7, with score excerpts of the bassoon, basses and violas. https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The violas hurry
cues.text: The violas take the bassoon’s phrase into the Allegro, adding quick descending notes and playing it short and detached. Second violas and cellos accompany them.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 7: Allegro non troppo, viola theme and accompaniment. https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Four days at the desk
cues.text: In February 1893 Tchaikovsky tells his nephew Vladimir Davydov that the first movement’s sketches are ready after less than four days. “You can’t imagine how blissful I feel,” he writes, “in the conviction that my time is not yet passed, and to work is still possible.”
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky to Vladimir Davydov, letter 4865, 11/23 February 1893, quoted in Tchaikovsky Research’s composition history. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6

cues.title: The strings sing
cues.text: Muted violins and cellos open the D-major melody. Tchaikovsky asks for tenderness, singing tone and breadth: teneramente, molto cantabile, con espansione. After all those short viola notes, the tune seems to take an enormous breath.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 8, reproduces the Andante string theme and its expression markings. The D-major second subject is also identified at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A secret for Davydov
cues.text: Tchaikovsky tells Davydov that the symphony has a programme which will remain an enigma: “Let them guess.” He also admits to weeping while composing it in his head on his travels. The finished score bears Davydov’s name as its dedicatee.
cues.evidence: Letter 4865 to Vladimir Davydov, 11/23 February 1893; dedication on the autograph score. Both are documented at https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6.

cues.title: Six pianissimos, then fortissimo
cues.text: The exposition ends with a bassoon line marked pppppp. The full orchestra breaks into that near-silence, and fast strings tear through pieces of the earlier tune. Tchaikovsky makes the join almost physically startling.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 10; Harlow Robinson’s Boston Symphony programme note describes the bassoon’s six-piano marking and the development’s orchestral attack. https://www.bso.org/works/tchaikovsky-symphony-no-6
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A funeral chant
cues.text: The brass carry a fragment of the Orthodox funeral service into the first movement. Its words ask Christ to give peace to the soul of his servant. In the score, the quotation occupies just four bars.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky Research identifies the Orthodox Requiem quotation in bars 202–205; Harlow Robinson’s Boston Symphony note identifies its brass scoring. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6 ; https://www.bso.org/works/tchaikovsky-symphony-no-6

cues.title: The song comes home
cues.text: The broad string melody returns in B major. The tune that first appeared in D now sings in the major version of the symphony’s home key, after the trombones and racing strings have spent their fury.
cues.evidence: The first movement’s B-major second-subject return is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky); orchestration and sequence in Queensland Symphony Orchestra’s learning resource, p. 10.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Plucked steps downwards
cues.text: The closing wind and brass phrases rest on descending pizzicato strings. B major holds, and the movement ends quietly, its last steps plucked instead of bowed.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 10, describes the wind and brass close over descending pizzicato strings. B-major coda: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The bassoon’s tune becomes a viola tune
transitions.how: At Allegro non troppo, the first violas reshape the bassoon phrase in B minor. Second violas and cellos accompany them; extra semiquavers and staccato dots turn the slow solo into a quick string tune.
transitions.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, pp. 5–7, compares the bassoon and viola themes. https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf

transitions.title: A pause before the strings sing
transitions.how: The quick music slows, and an ascending arpeggio passes from cellos to violas. After a pause, muted violins and cellos begin the D-major Andante. The instruction is teneramente, molto cantabile, con espansione: tenderly, very singing, with breadth.
transitions.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, pp. 7–8; D-major second subject and preceding caesura: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky).

transitions.title: The orchestra breaks the silence
transitions.how: A descending clarinet solo passes its last notes to the bassoon, marked pppppp. The full orchestra answers fortissimo. A half-diminished chord sends the harmony towards D minor, and the strings launch into the development.
transitions.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 10; development harmony: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky).

transitions.title: B major after the trombones
transitions.to: B′ · The melody in B major
transitions.how: The trombones’ climax subsides through bass and brass phrases. The strings recover the broad Andante tune in B major, changing the home key’s D♮ to D♯. Its long notes replace the preceding rush of semiquavers.
transitions.evidence: First-movement recapitulation and B-major return: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky); Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 10.

transitions.title: B major on plucked strings
transitions.from: B′ · The melody in B major
transitions.how: The returning melody quietens. Winds and brass carry the last phrases over pizzicato strings descending through the B-major close. The bowed song ends with small plucked steps beneath it.
transitions.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 10; the coda’s B major is identified at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky).

source.title: Tchaikovsky, Symphony No. 6, I, historical full-score scan
source.locator: PDF pp. 1–3 introduction; p. 12 Andante; pp. 20–43 central argument; pp. 44–51 lyrical return and close. Stage entries summarise broad passages, not every sounding part.

timeline.note: Opening passage: solo bassoon over divided basses; viola joins the low-register texture.
Latter introduction: winds, horns and cellos join the low strings (score PDF p. 2). The report’s 0:54 change anchors this broad state, not each entrance.
Allegro region: string figures carry the motif, with wind replies and horn support.
Andante region: muted violins and cellos share the broad melody; winds and horns support.
Reduced Adagio ending of the exposition: solo clarinet, quiet strings and timpani (score PDF p. 19); the report falls through 8:20–8:50. Placement is approximate.
The exposed bassoon continuation ends the exposition (score PDF p. 19). This brief reduced state is provisionally placed inside the very quiet 8:50–8:58 span, not bar-aligned.
Central argument: active strings are answered and reinforced by winds, brass and timpani across the passage.
Later lyrical return: the broad string line expands with wind and brass reinforcement.
Closing passage: softer wind harmony and a lightly articulated lower-string foundation replace the preceding breadth.

composer.epithet: He could make a ballroom glitter, then let one unguarded melody tell us who was unhappy there.
facts: School of Jurisprudence; Saint Petersburg Conservatory, 1862–65, with Anton Rubinstein and Nikolai Zaremba
Nadezhda von Meck: an allowance, 1877–90, and a friendship conducted by letter
Three ballets; Eugene Onegin, The Queen of Spades and other operas
composer.background:
At Kamenka on 6 July 1878, Tchaikovsky was explaining to Nadezhda von Meck how he composed. Ideas arrived in the middle of conversations; he held them in his head until he could sketch them on the first sheet of paper that came to hand. Waiting for the right mood was no way to work. “Inspiration is a guest who does not like to visit the idle,” he told her. Then he broke off for dinner. At two o’clock he resumed, moving on to sketching, orchestration, fair copies and how far a symphony must keep to its traditional form. Here is the composer of extravagant passions in his own voice: observant, companionable, exact about his trade.

He was born in Votkinsk, where his father managed an ironworks. He grew deeply attached to his French governess, Fanny Dürbach, and began piano lessons at the end of 1845. The profession chosen for him was the law. In 1850 he entered the preparatory class of the Imperial School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg. Four years later his mother died of cholera. He graduated in 1859 and took a post at the Ministry of Justice, while opera and concerts increasingly claimed his attention.
